source.title_on_document: Who performs better? Exploring the role of generative AI in creativity and brainstorming

supplement.where: The paper refers to no supplementary material or online appendix. Its own Appendix (Fig. 1, Table 1, Table 2) is part of this PDF on p. 9. The Data availability statement (p. 9) points to the OSF page with the preregistration and the data: https://osf.io/h6ztr/.
supplement.holds: Nothing beyond the main text. Every recorded statistic (F tests, eta squared, cell and marginal means and SDs, three 95% CIs) is printed in Sections 5.2-5.4 (pp. 6-7) and Table 1 (p. 9); cell ns are on p. 4. No standard errors are printed. The OSF page holds the preregistration and the data.

paper_design_summary: The in-person, 2 x 2 between-subjects lab experiment analyzed 212 undergraduates at a large Midwestern US public university who spent 10 minutes brainstorming improvements to the university's SOAR orientation program, either independently or with Microsoft Co-pilot, while anticipating a later human or AI teammate (pp. 4-5). Trained undergraduate coders blind to condition rated idea originality, feasibility, and fun on a 1-5 scale, averaged per participant; unique ideas and distinct categories were counted per participant (p. 5). The paper states random assignment to the four conditions, but anticipated teammate depended on session attendance: strangers attending the same session were paired, whereas participants attending alone anticipated AI; for paired participants, the unit of AI assignment is not specified (pp. 4-5).

studies.label: Lab experiment: SOAR brainstorming, 2 (independent vs AI-assisted ideation) x 2 (anticipated human vs AI teammate)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Ideation condition (independent vs AI-assisted with Microsoft Co-pilot), crossed with anticipated teammate (human vs AI) for a later group brainstorming session. The paper states random assignment to the four conditions (p. 4, Section 4), but anticipated teammate was set by session attendance: participants who signed up for and attended the same session were paired, were strangers, and anticipated each other; those who attended alone anticipated an AI teammate (p. 5, Section 4.2). The AI allocation mechanism is not described. For sessions attended alone, person and session coincide; for paired participants, the paper does not establish whether AI assistance was assigned per person or per session, or whether pair members could receive different ideation conditions. The unit is coded other to preserve this uncertainty, not to assert a particular allocation unit. The counts in the assignment sentence are analyzed cell counts.
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of the four conditions (Independent/Anticipated human teammate = 69; AI-assisted/Anticipated human teammate = 68; Independent/Anticipated AI teammate = 37; AI-assisted/Anticipated AI teammate = 38).
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 4 (Method); attendance-based anticipated teammate on p. 5, Section 4.2 (Study design); p. 9, Fig. 1 gives no allocation procedure

participants.exclusions: 224 participants were recruited and 212 were analyzed (p. 4, Section 4.1). Ten were excluded for failing condition-check items about their anticipated partner or receipt of AI assistance; these exclusions followed assignment. Two additional participants were excluded, one for a facilitator's failure to provide the required written handout and one for a language barrier affecting written ideas. Their timing relative to assignment is not explicitly stated, although the reasons concern the session procedure and written task. The recruitment and exclusion accounting is consistent with 224 assigned, but that total is implied rather than explicitly reported at assignment; n_randomized therefore remains null. The assignment sentence prints analyzed cell counts of 69/68/37/38, summing to 212, rather than a separate count at assignment. The paper gives no per-cell breakdown of the 12 exclusions, so all arm-level n_randomized values remain null.

ai_tool.name_model: Microsoft Co-pilot (Auto mode), university-licensed, accessed through individual accounts; underlying model not stated
ai_tool.how_used: Participants were instructed to use Co-pilot as an assisting tool, asking 'what' and 'how' questions for ideas or suggestions, and to type their own ideas rather than use AI-generated responses verbatim (p. 5, Sections 4.2-4.3). The scored ideas were typed in a Word document (p. 5, Section 4.4). Researchers gave step-by-step login instructions and assured participants that chat histories would be deleted immediately after data collection (p. 5, Section 4.3). No detailed usage or adherence measure for these instructions is reported.

task.description: Generate ideas to improve or redesign the university's Student Orientation, Advising, and Registration (SOAR) program to make it more engaging and helpful for future students; ideas typed into a Word document
task.duration: 10 minutes of individual idea generation (extended from 8 minutes after a pilot), after a 2-minute IDEO brainstorming video

outcomes.name: Originality of ideas (quality dimension)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Trained undergraduate coders blind to condition rated each idea on originality (novelty and uniqueness), 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent); participant score = mean over all of that participant's ideas. ICC .76 (first coding period, four coders, about 16% of ideas) and .84 (second period, about 20% of ideas). 2 x 2 ANOVA (SPSS 27) with Bonferroni-adjusted simple effects (p. 5, Section 4.4; p. 6, Section 4.5).

outcomes.name: Flexibility of ideas (number of distinct idea categories)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Coders blind to condition assigned each participant's ideas to a scheme of 13 mutually exclusive categories developed by the research team and coders; score = number of unique categories in the participant's list. Consistency was set by jointly coding the ideas of 15 participants and resolving discrepancies by consensus; no reliability statistic is reported (p. 5, Section 4.4). This is variety within one participant's ideas, not similarity across people.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is met on the explicit statement that participants were randomly assigned to the four conditions, including AI-assisted versus independent ideation (p. 4, Section 4); Co-pilot is identified as generative AI and was available during the scored task (pp. 4-5, Sections 4.2-4.3). The anticipated-teammate factor instead followed session attendance, so the four-cell statement is not accepted as evidence that teammate type was randomized (p. 5, Section 4.2). The source does not contradict random assignment of AI assistance, but its mechanism and the allocation unit for paired participants remain unreported; assignment.unit is other. Criterion 2 is met by 212 people analyzed, with analyzed cell counts 69/68/37/38 (p. 4, Sections 4-4.1); 106 per ideation condition is the sum of the relevant cells. Of 224 recruited, 12 were excluded; the total assigned is implied but not explicitly stated, and only the ten condition-check exclusions are clearly described as following assignment. Criterion 3 is met by blind coder ratings of originality, feasibility, and fun and counts of unique ideas and idea categories, all based on participant-produced output (p. 5, Section 4.4). Uncertain person-versus-session assignment affects the appropriate standard errors, but either randomization unit can satisfy criterion 1.

one_line_finding: Among 212 undergraduates analyzed, brainstorming with Microsoft Co-pilot raised coder-rated originality (3.34 vs 2.99; F(1, 208) = 16.78, p < .001) and fun (3.44 vs 3.18; p = .041) but lowered idea quantity (11.69 vs 13.24; p = .043) and category flexibility (6.06 vs 6.66; p = .026), with no main effect on feasibility (p = .101); the originality and fun gains were significant only among participants anticipating a human teammate (pp. 6-7; Table 1, p. 9).
open_questions: How was the AI-versus-independent ideation factor actually randomized across sessions and the two semesters within the larger project? The paper states random assignment (p. 4, Section 4), but its teammate factor followed session attendance (p. 5, Section 4.2). Authors' allocation protocol would clarify criterion 1; the current decision accepts the paper's explicit AI-assignment statement.

Could the two strangers paired within a session receive different ideation conditions, or was AI assistance assigned to their session? The PDF does not identify this unit. Authors' allocation records would settle the clustering needed for standard errors; either randomized unit is eligible.

What were the total and per-cell counts at assignment, the per-cell exclusions, and the timing of the two exclusions other than the ten condition-check failures? The paper reports 224 recruited and 212 analyzed (p. 4, Section 4.1), implying but not explicitly reporting the total assigned. Authors' allocation and exclusion records would settle this without changing the confirmed analyzed count.

Are the printed eta-squared values partial eta-squared, and do the main-effect F tests use weighted or unweighted marginal means? Section 4.5 (p. 6) names ANOVA, estimated marginal means for follow-up comparisons, Bonferroni adjustment, and SPSS 27, but not the main-effect weighting or eta-squared definition. The checker's arithmetic interpretation is not an explicit source statement; authors' original SPSS syntax or output would settle it.

Which outcome, if any, does the OSF preregistration name as primary? The paper's preregistered Hypothesis 1 covers quantity, quality, and flexibility together (p. 3), and no primary outcome is named in the PDF. Inspect the preregistration linked at https://osf.io/h6ztr/ (p. 9, Data availability).
notes: Single study. Outcome order follows the paper's quality dimensions (originality, feasibility, fun), then quantity and flexibility; screener B numbered fun S1-O2 and feasibility S1-O3. Impression management (five 7-point self-report items, used as a manipulation check) is not scored on the output and is not listed; it showed no ideation-condition effect, F(1, 208) = .413, p = .521 (p. 6, Section 5.1). Main effects of anticipated teammate (Table 1: originality 3.24 vs 3.04, fun 3.45 vs 3.06) do not vary AI assistance, and that factor was set by arrival, so they are not listed as contrasts. Flexibility counts categories within one participant's ideas, so there is no across_people outcome, although the Discussion speaks of 'idea diversity'. No outcome from the anticipated group session is reported, so there is no after_ai outcome. Raters were trained undergraduate coders, coded human_raters. All statistics come from 2 x 2 ANOVAs in SPSS 27 with Bonferroni-adjusted simple effects; no standard errors are printed. The simple-effect error df (135 and 73) equal each teammate group's n minus 2. Table 1 prints no ns; cell ns are on p. 4. Effect sizes are labeled η² and are not counted as standardized_effect (see reconciliation). Table 1 was checked on the PDF page image because the markdown scrambles it. Finalization read the entire markdown, including the Appendix and references, and checked the numerical source passages in PDF pp. 1, 3-9; all eleven contrast values were retained. The uncertainty about person-versus-session AI assignment must be resolved before assuming that participant-level standard errors account for the independent assignment units. The original eta-squared labels and the separately reported Table 1 descriptive means and main-effect tests are retained without inferring a statistical specification. The unchanged reconciliation object records earlier judgments; the final corrections to assignment unit, pairing wording, instructions, and exclusion timing supersede its corresponding historical statements.

challenge_resolution.quote: A total of 224 participants were recruited for this in-person lab experiment at a large public university in the Midwestern United States.
challenge_resolution.locator: p. 4, Section 4.1 (Participants) and Section 4 (analyzed cell counts in assignment sentence); p. 5, Sections 4.2-4.3 (session procedure)

open_items.item: Open question 1: Actual AI-assignment mechanism across sessions, semesters, and the larger project. This bears on criterion 1, currently met from the explicit random-assignment statement; authors should confirm the allocation protocol and that AI access itself was randomized (pp. 4-5).

Open question 2: Person-versus-session AI assignment among paired strangers. Authors should confirm whether pair members could receive different AI conditions. This determines clustering for standard errors; either randomized unit can satisfy criterion 1, so it does not independently change eligibility (p. 5, Section 4.2; p. 9, Fig. 1).

Open question 3: Explicit total and per-cell counts at assignment, exclusion cells, and the timing of the two non-condition-check exclusions. Authors should provide allocation and exclusion records. Criterion 2 is settled by 212 people analyzed, independently of the unstated randomized counts (p. 4, Sections 4-4.1).

Open question 4: Whether the printed eta-squared values are partial and which marginal means the main-effect F tests compare. The PDF does not explicitly specify either; retain all printed labels and values. Original SPSS syntax or output from the authors would settle this extraction issue. Numerical consistency alone is not a source statement (p. 6, Section 4.5 and Section 5.3; p. 9, Table 1).

Open question 5: Any preregistered primary outcome. Inspect the preregistration in the posted OSF materials linked at https://osf.io/h6ztr/ (p. 9, Data availability); it was not inspected during finalization. The paper names no primary outcome, so primary remains not_stated. This affects selection of an estimate, not any eligibility criterion.
